blocks.text: Pharmacokinetics is the time course and disposition of drugs in the body (what the body does to the drug). It differs to some extent with the route of administration.

Commonly used routes for psychotropic drugs: oral, intramuscular, intravenous and rectal. Inhalation, topical, subcutaneous, sublingual and intra-arterial routes are possible but not generally used in psychiatric practice.
Pharmacokinetics involves the processes of **ADME**: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism and Elimination.

blocks.note: **Q52**: the enhancement of drug effects after repeated administration of the same dose is sensitisation (explanation: the physiological opposite of tolerance, seen in drug addiction; tolerance is diminished response after repeated exposure). Not covered in the notes.

bullets.text: Pharmacokinetics = time course and disposition of drugs in the body (what the body does to the drug); it varies with route of administration.
Routes commonly used for psychotropics: oral, IM, IV, rectal. Inhalation, topical, SC, sublingual, intra-arterial are not generally used in psychiatry.
The processes are ADME: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Elimination.

blocks.text: Route of administration and chemical properties of a drug influence absorption. Rate of absorption is affected by the form of the drug (e.g. enteric coating slows tablet disintegration in the stomach), by blood flow at the site of administration (higher blood flow, greater absorption rate) and by solubility (depends on pH of the drug, size of particles in the formulation and the pKa of the drug).
pKa is the pH at which precisely half of the drug is in its ionized form.

Oral administration is one of the most common routes. It leads to a variable plasma concentration, as absorption may be erratic and subject to metabolism by liver and gut mucosa (first-pass effect); drugs absorbed from the gut undergo extensive metabolism before entering the systemic circulation.
The main mechanisms of absorption from the **GI** tract are active transport, passive diffusion (the most common mechanism) and pore filtration.

Presence of food delays gastric emptying; anticholinergic activity of some psychotropics (tricyclic antidepressants, opiates etc.) can delay gastric emptying

blocks.title: Factors influencing absorption from the GI tract

blocks.text: Poor oral absorption leads to lower bioavailability in plasma compared with intravenous administration. This is mainly due to lack of absorption from the intestine, related to inhibitory factors such as food or gastric acid, or to changes in intestinal motility.

Site of absorption: the small intestine is less acidic than the stomach and most absorption takes place there, aided by a large surface area and long transit time. Although oral absorption occurs primarily in the small intestine, absorption of many slow or sustained release drugs occurs in the large bowel.

P-glycoprotein: a reverse transporter that pumps certain drug molecules actively out into the gut lumen from the gut cells and so can affect absorption. Inhibition of P-glycoprotein (e.g. by grapefruit juice) can increase absorption of certain medications.

The grapefruit juice effect is due to bergamottin, 6,7-dihydroxybergamottin and naringenin, which significantly increase oral bioavailability by selectively and rapidly down-regulating intestinal (but not liver) **CYP3A4** and, to a lesser extent, **CYP1A2**.

The grapefruit effect is greatest for drugs with high first-pass metabolism: the calcium antagonists felodipine and nimodipine, terfenadine, **carbamazepine**, triazolam and midazolam (to some extent **diazepam**), simvastatin and methylprednisone. Grapefruit also significantly affects **buspirone** and pimozide.

Special preparations: with oral dosing, rate and sometimes extent of absorption are largely determined by disintegration and dissolution of the dosage form. Tablets and capsules must disintegrate to expose a greater surface area; enteric coating slows disintegration, which is also prolonged by hard compaction or wax in a drug matrix.

Modified release preparations prolong drug effects and reduce peak plasma concentrations, and so may reduce side effects (e.g. **lithium**, **carbamazepine**, sodium **valproate**, **quetiapine** XL).
Liquids or syrups are absorbed more quickly than tablets because disintegration and dissolution are not required.
Dissolution rate depends on: (1) size of drug particle, (2) solubility of the drug, (3) properties of intestinal fluid (e.g. pH).

bullets.text: Absorption rate depends on drug form (enteric coating slows disintegration), blood flow at site (higher flow, faster) and solubility (pH, particle size, pKa).
Oral route gives variable plasma levels (erratic absorption; first-pass metabolism by liver and gut mucosa). Passive diffusion is the most common GI mechanism.
Most absorption is in the small intestine (less acidic, large surface area, long transit time); slow/sustained-release drugs may be absorbed in the large bowel.
P-glycoprotein pumps drugs back into the gut lumen; grapefruit juice inhibits it and down-regulates intestinal (not liver) CYP3A4, raising bioavailability of high first-pass drugs.
Modified release (lithium, carbamazepine, valproate, quetiapine XL) lowers peaks and may reduce side effects; liquids absorb faster than tablets.
IM absorption takes 10-30 minutes and avoids most first pass; IV is fastest, no first pass, 100% bioavailable, higher risk of sudden life-threatening effects.

blocks.text: Permeation is the lipid membrane permeability of the drug molecule. After oral administration a drug may be incompletely absorbed, e.g. only ==40%== of a dose of **chlorpromazine** reaches the systemic circulation, mainly due to lack of absorption from the gut.

Lipophilicity: highly hydrophilic drugs cannot cross the lipid cell membrane, while highly lipophilic drugs struggle to cross the water layer in the extracellular space. **Atenolol** is too hydrophilic to be absorbed easily and has low bioavailability.

Concentration gradient also affects permeation; only free drug forms contribute to it, so protein binding indirectly affects permeation. Surface area and vascularity of the gut mucosa are important for absorption.

rows: Along the concentration gradient without any specific transport mechanism
Along the concentration gradient but facilitated by carrier-specific mechanisms
Against the concentration gradient; **ATP** dependent energy expenditure
blocks.title: Types of permeation

blocks.text: Only the nonionized form of a drug can cross the lipid membranes of a cell. Many drugs are weak acids or weak bases and exist in nonionized and ionized forms in equilibrium, depending on environmental pH and the drug's pKa (the pH at which the molecule is split into ==50%== ionized and ==50%== nonionized forms).

The ionized form is more water-soluble than the nonionized form, so ionized drug is trapped in the glomerular filtrate and not reabsorbed; renal clearance is higher for ionized drugs. A weak base can be ionized by acidifying urine; a weak acid by alkalinising urine.

rows: May help elimination, but complications of the procedure often override benefits

**Q61**: a drug highly permeable across lipid membranes with high oral bioavailability needs balanced hydrophilic and lipophilic properties. Per the explanation, a highly hydrophilic drug cannot cross the lipid membrane and a highly lipophilic one cannot cross the water layer next to the cell.

bullets.text: Permeation = lipid membrane permeability of the drug; e.g. only 40% of oral chlorpromazine reaches the systemic circulation.
Highly hydrophilic drugs cannot cross the lipid membrane (atenolol); highly lipophilic drugs struggle to cross the extracellular water layer.
Simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion run down the concentration gradient; active transport is against it and uses ATP.
Only nonionized drug crosses lipid membranes; pKa is the pH at which 50% is ionized and 50% nonionized.
Ionized drug is trapped in glomerular filtrate, so renal clearance is higher for ionized drugs.
Alkalinise urine for salicylate and barbiturate overdose; acidify for amphetamines and phencyclidine (complications often outweigh benefit).

sections.title: 4. Distribution (C): protein binding and volume of distribution

blocks.text: Distribution refers to where in the body a drug can be found. Drugs are not evenly distributed: some are confined to body fluids, others accumulate in particular tissues.

rows: Cardiac output, regional blood flow. Organs with the highest perfusion (brain, kidneys, liver) receive the highest distribution; redistribution in the second phase is to skeletal muscle, adipose tissue and skin
Higher the lipid solubility, the greater the rate of entry into cells
blocks.title: Factors influencing distribution

blocks.text: Distribution is the drug achieving equilibrium between compartments. In the two compartment model the body is divided into a central compartment (plasma) and a peripheral compartment (fat and other tissues, varying with age, sex and weight). Distribution lowers plasma concentration (central to peripheral shift) and is most rapid after intravenous administration.

Protein binding: the unbound (free) fraction is the active fraction (binds receptors, crosses the blood-brain barrier). Reduced protein binding increases the free fraction and therefore the effect of the drug.

Plasma protein binding is usually reversible, so changes can have profound effects on drug availability. Drugs highly protein bound (>==90%==) such as **phenytoin** are most prone to interactions: **diazepam** displaces **phenytoin** from plasma proteins, raising free **phenytoin** and the risk of adverse effects.

Effects of protein displacement are usually not clinically significant, because metabolism of the affected drug rises in parallel with free drug; the free level rises briefly then returns to the previous steady state, so untoward effects are normally short-lived.
Protein binding interactions become relevant in renal disease where proteinuria can occur.

rows: Principal plasma protein binding acidic drugs
Primary binding protein for alkaline drugs; most psychotropics are basic and may bind it and lipoproteins
blocks.title: Plasma proteins and binding percentages

blocks.text: Volume of distribution: Vd = Q/Cp, where Vd is volume of distribution, Q is quantity of drug and Cp is plasma concentration at the time of administration ('zero time').
Vd is an apparent (not true) volume. The higher the Vd, the lower the plasma concentration. A high Vd indicates high affinity for tissues outside body water such as brain and fat.

A low Vd (say 10 or 20 litres) suggests the drug is concentrated in the blood itself; a high Vd (say 500 or 1000 litres) suggests it is concentrated in cells or fatty tissues and not the blood. Increased lipid solubility is associated with increased Vd, which is the case for most psychotropic drugs at physiological pH.

A highly protein-bound drug has high plasma concentration and therefore lower Vd (restricted by total plasma volume). Tissue binding (fat or muscle) and accumulation gives low plasma concentration and so a high Vd; hence competition for protein binding can alter Vd.
**Q55**: Vd calculation. **IV** 10 mg giving a plasma concentration of 0.01 mg/mL immediately after administration; the answer is 1000 mL, by Vd = Q/Cp as given in the explanation.

bullets.text: Distribution = where in the body the drug is found; uneven, some drugs stay in body fluids while others accumulate in tissues.
Influences: haemodynamic factors, plasma protein binding, permeability (lipid solubility), blood-brain barrier, blood-CSF barrier.
Only the unbound (free) fraction is active; reduced protein binding raises free fraction and effect.
Protein-binding interactions (e.g. diazepam displacing phenytoin) are usually short-lived because metabolism rises with the free level; relevant in renal disease with proteinuria.
Albumin binds acidic drugs; alpha-1 acid glycoprotein binds alkaline drugs (most psychotropics are basic).
Vd = Q/Cp (apparent volume). High Vd = lipophilic / tissue-bound drug with low plasma concentration; high protein binding = lower Vd.

blocks.text: Distribution of a drug to the brain is governed by 3 factors: (1) the brain's regional blood flow, (2) the blood-brain barrier, (3) the drug's affinity for receptors in the brain.
The blood-brain barrier is a structural and functional barrier comprising the capillary endothelium of the brain, which possesses tight junctions, acting in unison as a single sheet or membrane.

The barrier prevents proteins and other molecules such as immunoglobulins from entering or leaving the brain's blood supply. It also protects the brain from bacteria and viruses, maintains an osmotic gradient and keeps the cerebral glucose compartment different from the periphery.

Factors that could affect **BBB** permeability: fever, head injury, hypoxia, hypercapnia, retroviruses, inflammation, vasculitis, hypertension, cerebral irradiation and aging. Integrity can be measured by leakiness to labeled IgG molecules or gadolinium.

The ability of a drug to cross the **BBB** depends on molecular size, lipid solubility and ionic status. Unionized molecules that are freely available and less protein bound cross easily; in general the higher the lipid-water partition coefficient, the greater the ability to cross.

rows: Specific carrier mechanisms (amino acid transport system is stereospecific: l- not d-amino acids are easily transferred)
Some small molecules, e.g. **lithium**, diffuse readily into the brain and **CSF** from the cerebral circulation
blocks.title: Drugs crossing the BBB despite low lipid-water partition coefficient

blocks.text: Circumventricular organs around the ventricles lack a **BBB**, e.g. the subfornical organ, area postrema of the medulla and the median eminence; they allow transfer of many compounds from blood to brain. A possible survival benefit: certain toxic substances stimulate the area postrema and induce nausea and vomiting.

There is no evidence that inhaled medications bypass the **BBB**; to some extent nasal sprays can reach the brain via olfactory epithelium and bypass it. Anaesthetic agents do not increase **BBB** permeability.
A blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier also exists, at the choroid plexus. Here the tight junctions lie between adjacent epithelial cells, as opposed to adjacent endothelial cells in the **BBB**.

**Q68**: the factor that decides **BBB** permeability is the lipid-water partition coefficient (not frequency/time of administration, half-life or nitrogen content). The explanation repeats that size, lipid solubility and ionic status matter and that unionized, freely available, less protein-bound molecules cross easily.

bullets.text: Brain distribution depends on regional blood flow, the BBB, and the drug's affinity for brain receptors.
BBB = brain capillary endothelium with tight junctions acting as a single membrane; it blocks proteins/immunoglobulins and protects against bacteria and viruses.
BBB permeability is affected by fever, head injury, hypoxia, hypercapnia, retroviruses, inflammation, vasculitis, hypertension, cerebral irradiation, aging.
Crossing depends on size, lipid solubility, ionic status; higher lipid-water partition coefficient = better crossing. L-dopa, l-tryptophan and valproate use carriers; lithium diffuses in.
Circumventricular organs (subfornical organ, area postrema, median eminence) lack a BBB.
Blood-CSF barrier is at the choroid plexus, with tight junctions between epithelial (not endothelial) cells.

blocks.text: Bioavailability is how much of an administered drug reaches its target: the extent to which the drug reaches the systemic circulation after oral or parenteral administration, compared with the same quantity given intravenously; the fraction that circumvents first pass and reaches the systemic circulation.

**AUC** (area under the plasma concentration-time curve) after a single dose is proportional to the amount of drug in plasma and gives the fraction of dose absorbed. Bioavailability fraction = **AUC** after oral dose divided by **AUC** after **IV** administration of the same dose.
Bioavailability is determined by three factors: absorption, distribution, elimination (metabolism and/or excretion).

**IV** administration gives ==100%== availability. This is not so for extravascular routes (oral, rectal, inhalational, intramuscular, subcutaneous); the reduction relates to degree of absorption and 'first-pass' (presystemic) metabolism, prominent in gut mucosa, liver and to some extent muscle. This explains why higher doses are needed orally than intramuscularly.

columns: Proportion of oral dose entering systemic circulation
blocks.title: Examples of high first-pass metabolism

blocks.text: Hepatic impairment can reduce first-pass metabolism, requiring dosage adjustment of drugs metabolized by the liver.

Bioequivalence: comparability of plasma levels of two formulations of the same active compound at the same dose and route. Two products are bioequivalent when their plasma level-time plots are superimposable, which needs the same bioavailability and rate of absorption. It matters when changing brand, e.g. camcolit vs priadel (**lithium** carbonate) or Clozaril vs zaponex (**clozapine**).

sections.title: 7. Metabolism of drugs (E) and the CYP450 system

blocks.text: Biotransformation renders a drug less lipid-soluble and more water-soluble, so products are more readily eliminated. The liver is the principal site, but metabolism can occur in the **GI** tract, plasma, lungs, kidneys, suprarenal cortex, placenta, skin and lymphocytes. The four major routes are oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis and conjugation.

blocks.title: Phase 1 vs Phase 2 metabolism
rows: A molecule (active or inactive) suitable for conjugation
Polar compounds (mostly inactive) excretable in bile or urine
Renal if relative molecular mass is less than 300; bile if more than 300

blocks.text: Because **oxazepam** bypasses phase 1, in alcoholic liver disease **oxazepam** is favoured for alcohol detoxification instead of **chlordiazepoxide**, which requires intact liver enzymes for phase 1 clearance. Metabolism usually yields inactive, more polar metabolites but can convert inactive pro-drugs into active metabolites.

Most psychotherapeutic drugs are oxidized by the hepatic cytochrome P-450 system. The most studied is **CYP2D6**; together with **CYP3A4** it makes up nearly ==90%== of all psychotropic metabolism. **CYP** enzymes inactivate most psychotherapeutic drugs and act primarily in the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes and intestinal cells, so viral hepatitis or cirrhosis may affect efficiency.
There are 3 ways drug interactions may influence the **CYP** system: induction, non-competitive inhibition and competitive inhibition.
Genetic variation: between 5 and ==10%== of Caucasians lack **CYP2D6** and are poor metabolizers of its substrates; up to 15-==20%== of East Asians are poor metabolizers of **CYP2C19** substrates.

rows: **Paroxetine**, to some extent **fluoxetine**, neuroleptics, **amitriptyline** and **clomipramine** inhibit 2D6
Stimulated by **carbamazepine** and barbiturates; inhibited by calcium channel blockers, **fluoxetine** and **nefazodone**. Smoking induces **CYP1A2** via **PAH**

Most antidepressants can inhibit warfarin metabolism via a complex mechanism, with potentially serious bleeding
Compete for the same metabolic enzymes
Alcohol, smoking and brussel sprouts are **CYP** inducers; grapefruit juice and caffeine inhibit the **CYP** system

blocks.text: Autoinduction: **carbamazepine** is metabolized by hepatic **CYP2D6**, synthesis of which it induces. Metabolism of **carbamazepine** (and other **P450** substrates) gradually increases over the first several weeks. The initial steady state may be reached in 4 to 5 days but final steady state may be delayed until 3 to 4 weeks after starting; so **carbamazepine** levels must be monitored and the dose often raised early. **Chlorpromazine** can also induce its own metabolism to some extent.

Smoking and caffeine affect glucuronidation (via **UGT**) and **CYP1A2**. Drugs not dependent on **CYP1A2** or **UGT** are unaffected: **risperidone** and **aripiprazole** (**CYP2D6** and **CYP3A**), **quetiapine** (mainly **CYP3A**), **ziprasidone** (mainly aldehyde oxidase and **CYP3A**).

**Clozapine** and **olanzapine** metabolism depends mainly on **CYP1A2** and UGTs. Caffeine competitively inhibits **CYP1A2**, raising **clozapine** and **olanzapine** levels, while polyaromatic hydrocarbons (**PAH**) in cigarettes induce the enzyme. Inhibitor effects (caffeine) are seen sooner than inducer effects (smoking), which need fresh synthesis of **CYP1A2** enzymes (de Leon, 2004).

Alcohol breakdown: four distinct pathways, 3 oxidative and 1 non-oxidative. Each oxidative pathway oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde, then to acetate for extra-hepatic activation to acetyl-CoA. Pathway 1 (cytoplasmic alcohol dehydrogenase) accounts for >==90%== of breakdown in Caucasians; pathway 2 uses the endoplasmic reticulum Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System (**MEOS** or **CYP450** 2E1); pathway 3 uses peroxisomal catalase.
The nonoxidative pathway for ethanol is less well characterized and produces fatty acid ethyl esters (FAEEs) as primary end products.

bullets.text: Metabolism makes drugs less lipid- and more water-soluble; liver is the principal site. Four routes: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis, conjugation.
Phase 1 = oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis (CYP). Phase 2 = conjugation (glucuronidation); conjugates <300 relative molecular mass go renal, >300 go bile.
Lorazepam, temazepam and oxazepam go straight to phase 2, so oxazepam is favoured over chlordiazepoxide in alcoholic liver disease.
CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 account for nearly 90% of psychotropic metabolism.
Poor metabolizers: 5-10% of Caucasians lack CYP2D6; up to 15-20% of East Asians are CYP2C19 poor metabolizers.
Fluvoxamine can raise clozapine 10-fold (seizure risk); carbamazepine lowers many drugs incl. OCP; carbamazepine and phenobarbitone induce their own metabolism.
Carbamazepine autoinduction: steady state at 4-5 days initially but final steady state 3-4 weeks in; monitor levels and raise dose.
Smoking (PAH) induces and caffeine inhibits CYP1A2, changing clozapine/olanzapine levels; risperidone, aripiprazole, quetiapine, ziprasidone are unaffected.

blocks.text: Major excretion routes are urine, faeces and bile. Psychotropic drugs are also excreted in sweat, sebum, tears, saliva and breast milk. Both active forms and inactive metabolites can be excreted. Ionized and non-lipid soluble compounds are best suited to renal excretion.

rows: Normally weakly acidic, good for excretion of tricyclics and amphetamines; alkaline diuresis is needed to enhance elimination of aspirin or phenobarbitone in overdose
Increases **lithium** reabsorption and decreases excretion, causing toxicity
blocks.title: Factors influencing excretion

blocks.text: Clearance is the rate of elimination of a drug: the volume of blood cleared of a particular drug in unit time. Total body clearance depends on renal and nonrenal clearance (sweat, bile etc.).
Clearance is directly proportional to volume of distribution: Cl = k x Vd, where k is the first order elimination constant.

Clearance is specific for each drug and does not depend on plasma concentration (elimination rises as concentration rises under first order kinetics). For first order drugs clearance is constant irrespective of dose consumed, because rate of elimination is directly proportional to plasma level.

Renal elimination without significant liver breakdown is seen for **lithium**, **amisulpride**, **sulpiride**, **gabapentin**, **acamprosate** and amantadine. **Sulpiride** and **amisulpride** have up to ==90%== elimination via the renal route, a minor portion via the biliary system; **amisulpride** produces 2 weak metabolites after limited hepatic breakdown.
Half-life (t1/2) is the time taken for plasma concentration of a drug to halve.

After **IV** injection there is a rapid fall in plasma concentration caused by redistribution into other tissues; the time for this to halve the initial peak is the distribution half-life. The time for elimination to halve plasma concentration is the elimination half-life, which is what clinicians are usually interested in.

blocks.title: Distribution half-life vs elimination half-life
rows: Redistribution of drug from blood to other tissues after **IV** injection
Time to halve the initial peak concentration by redistribution
Time for elimination to halve plasma concentration

blocks.text: First order worked example in the notes: if t1/2 is 2 hours for drug A, plasma concentration goes 100 mg/ml, then 50 mg/ml after 2 hours, 25 mg/ml after 2 more hours, then 12.5 mg/ml.

Zero order worked example in the notes: 100 mg, then 80 mg after 2 hours, 60 mg, then 40 mg; i.e. a constant 20 mg is metabolized every 2 hours. Certain drugs undergo zero order kinetics even at therapeutic doses.
In that zero order example the apparent 'half-life' of a 100 mg dose is about 5 hours, but of an 80 mg dose only 4 hours.

rows: Enzyme saturation: first order elimination switches to zero order
blocks.title: Examples of zero order behaviour

blocks.text: Steady state: with episodic dosing, plasma values rise after each dose and fall, but the next dose is given before levels reach a flat trough, so levels build up gradually. It takes 4-5 t1/2 to reach steady plasma level. At steady state fluctuations persist but the average concentration between two successive doses stays the same; steady state is reached when rate in = rate out.

blocks.text: Quantal curves plot the percentage of a population showing a specified, predefined categorical drug effect against dose or log dose. The dose-response curve plots drug concentration against the continuous effects of the drug.

These curves give the median effective dose and median toxic dose: median toxic dose = dose at which ==50%== of patients experience a specific toxic effect; median effective dose = dose at which ==50%== have a specified therapeutic effect.
Steep dose-response curves reflect little intersubject variability; flat curves indicate great variability in patient sensitivity.

Therapeutic index is the relative measure of toxicity or safety: the ratio of median toxic dose to median effective dose (equivalently, the ratio of minimum plasma concentration causing toxic effects to that causing a therapeutic effect). It varies with the toxic symptom specified; e.g. gastrointestinal toxicity of **lithium** can occur at a lower plasma concentration than seizures.

In the lab it is determined using median lethal dose (**LD50**) and median toxic dose (**TD50**) in animals; in humans using 'minimal' effective and 'minimal' toxic doses from trial data. It is only relevant to dose-dependent side effects, not idiosyncratic reactions.

Therapeutic index range: **lithium**, **carbamazepine** and **phenytoin** have a narrow range of plasma levels within which efficacy is optimum and toxicity less evident; above it toxicity rises, below it efficacy falls. Drugs with a low therapeutic index or narrow therapeutic range require plasma monitoring.

blocks.text: Kidney mass is reported to fall by approximately 20 to ==25%== between age 30 and 80 years. Renal blood flow reduces with age even in healthy people, by about ==10%== per decade after the age of 20. By age 80, **RBF** may be 600 ml/min compared with 1200 ml/min in young adults.

Creatinine measurements can be spurious, so **GFR** formulas must correct for age and other variables. Nearly ==40%== of renal function is lost by age 80; the average decline is around 10 mL/min/1.73m2 per decade after age 30, taking adult **GFR** from 130 mL/min/1.73m2 to 80 mL/min/1.73m2 at age 80 (The Baltimore Longitudinal Study).

blocks.text: Tricyclics are orally well absorbed but have variable time to peak plasma concentration (1 to 12 h). Many have active metabolites. Most have a long half-life (close to 24 h) that allows once-daily dosing, and readily cross lipid barriers such as the blood-brain barrier and placenta. They are extensively bound to plasma proteins, e.g. **imipramine** 80-==95%==.

Nearly 7-==9%== of Caucasians are slow metabolizers of tricyclics (debrisoquin hydroxylation) because of **CYP2D6** polymorphism; up to a 40 times difference in plasma **TCA** concentrations can occur. Children clear more tricyclics, the elderly clear less.

**TCA** monitoring: plasma (not serum) levels are measured, after 5-7 days when steady state is reached, and 8-12 hrs after the last dose to avoid false peaks while absorption is occurring. **Imipramine** and desipramine show a sigmoidal curve where dose-response plateaus; **nortriptyline** has a clear therapeutic window of 50 to 150 ng/ml. This inverted U is not due to decreased responsivity secondary to side-effects.
**Amitriptyline** and **clomipramine** decrease the metabolism of morphine and may contribute to opioid toxicity through **UDP** glucuronyl transferase interaction (Chadwick 2005).

blocks.text: SSRIs are rapidly absorbed; **sertraline** availability may be increased by the presence of food. Most are highly protein bound except **escitalopram** (==56%== bound).

**Fluoxetine** is metabolized to norfluoxetine, which has similar activity on 5-**HT** reuptake as **fluoxetine**. Norfluoxetine half-life is 4-16 days while **fluoxetine**'s is 4-6 days. **Sertraline**'s metabolite has a longer half-life but, unlike norfluoxetine, is not a potent reuptake inhibitor. Desmethylcitalopram is a potent noradrenaline uptake inhibitor but is not produced sufficiently and weakly crosses the blood-brain barrier. **Fluvoxamine** and **paroxetine** have no active metabolites.

**Fluoxetine** and **paroxetine** can inhibit their own clearance at clinically relevant doses, so have nonlinear pharmacokinetics: changes in dose can produce proportionately large plasma levels. Half-life is not related to time to onset of action but is relevant for discontinuation reactions.

Selectivity: **citalopram** (and **escitalopram**) are the most selective; **paroxetine** is the most potent. **Fluoxetine** weakly inhibits noradrenaline reuptake and binds 5-**HT2C** receptors; **sertraline** weakly inhibits noradrenaline and dopamine reuptake. **Paroxetine** has significant anticholinergic activity at higher dosages and binds nitric oxide synthase. **Fluoxetine** plus **olanzapine** increases brain noradrenaline.

Dosing: apart from depression and **GAD**, panic disorder, **OCD**, **OCD** spectrum disorders and bulimia respond to SSRIs. **OCD** may need a higher dose for several months. **Fluoxetine** treatment of bulimia is best given with psychotherapy, at higher dosages. In premenstrual dysphoria (**PMDD**) **sertraline** or **paroxetine** daily or only in the luteal phase is positive; intermittent dosing is usually as effective as continuous; benefit is seen in one to two days but proof of efficacy is lacking.

**Fluvoxamine** reduces clearance of **diazepam** and its active metabolite N-desmethyldiazepam, with likely substantial accumulation, so they should not ordinarily be co-administered. **Citalopram** is metabolized by **CYP2C19** initially and then **CYP2D6**; **CYP3A3** and **CYP3A4** demethylate **sertraline**.

blocks.text: **Lithium** is orally well absorbed and not metabolized in the liver; it is renally excreted. **Lithium** carbonate and citrate are not bioequivalent preparations. It is rapidly and completely absorbed, takes 4-5 days to reach steady state in healthy young males, and is not protein bound. Plasma half-life is around 18 hours initially, rising to 36 hours after 1 year of chronic use.

**Lithium** is excreted via the proximal tubules where sodium is also filtered, so any loss of body sodium can increase **lithium** reabsorption in error, leading to toxicity; sodium homeostasis is important.

**Valproate** is available as semisodium compound (**divalproex**, half valproic acid and half sodium **valproate**, somewhat better tolerated) and as sodium salt of valproic acid. It is well absorbed, bioavailability close to ==100%==, quite hydrophilic with a low volume of distribution.

**Valproate**: t1/2 9 to 16 hours; highly (==90%==) protein bound, with saturable binding so at higher doses a greater percentage is free; the increased free fraction stays in plasma and is cleared by the liver, giving 'sublinear' kinetics (greater dose increases needed for desired plasma level increases). **VPA** can increase free **diazepam** through binding interactions.

**Carbamazepine**: tricyclic structure, hepatic metabolism, erratic absorption, bioavailability about ==80%==, about ==75%== plasma protein bound; it induces its own breakdown. Before autoinduction (epoxide pathway via **CYP3A3**/4) half-life is about 24 hr and clearance about 25 mL/min; after autoinduction (2 to 4 weeks into therapy) half-life falls to about 8 hr and clearance rises to about 75 mL/min.

The active **CBZ-10**,11-epoxide metabolite has a half-life of about 6 hr. Conventional **carbamazepine** needs multiple divided doses; extended release can be twice a day. Steady-state plasma concentration of 4 to 12 ng/ml is therapeutic (as stated in the notes).

blocks.text: **Gabapentin** has no significant mood stabilizing effects though useful for anxiety in bipolar patients. Not protein bound, not metabolized, ==100%== excreted in urine. Half-life about 6 hrs (4 to 9); clearance similar to creatinine (120 ml/min), so increased physical activity may increase clearance. Bioavailability is not dose-proportional: about ==60%== at 900 mg/day (3 divided doses), ==34%== at 2400 mg/day and ==27%== at 4800 mg/day.

**Gabapentin** does not induce or inhibit hepatic metabolism, has linear kinetics at usual dosages, so drug-drug interactions are not an issue. blocks.text: Depot kinetics (box on page 30): some long-acting injections (such as **risperidone**, **pipotiazine**) show delayed as well as prolonged release and need adequate oral antipsychotic cover after the first dose. blocks.text: **Diazepam**: well absorbed orally, bioavailability nearly ==100%==; peak in 15-90 minutes with a second peak at 6-12 hours due to enterohepatic recirculation. Highly lipophilic (**CSF** concentration more or less equals plasma), 95-==99%== protein bound. Slow elimination t1/2 30 h (range 20-100 h); steady state takes 5-6 days. Extensively metabolized in the liver to 3 active metabolites: nordiazepam/desmethyldiazepam (principal; could accumulate), **oxazepam** and **temazepam**.

Z-hypnotics: **zolpidem**, zaleplon and eszopiclone are quickly and completely absorbed orally; food may delay absorption by an hour. Lack of active metabolites avoids accumulation and hangover effects. **NICE**'s appraisal committee concluded no compelling evidence of a clinically useful difference between Z-drugs and short-acting benzodiazepines in effectiveness, adverse effects or misuse/dependence potential, but this is controversial.
